title: Prepare Upstream for a Major Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post advises leaders facing a high-stakes decision to start talking weeks or months ahead, not about the decision itself but about its nature. It begins with the question of why the decision needs to be made at all, which is easier to ask impartially when no deadline is pressing. Teams should also surface and challenge their assumptions about markets, customers, competitors and costs, and define what success would look like. With time to spare, risks and unintended consequences can be discussed more openly. The author closes with Muhammad Ali's line about running on the road long before dancing under the lights.
points: Discuss the nature of a decision long before the analysis starts, not the decision itself.
Asking why the decision is needed is more impartial when there is no time pressure.
Early work should expose assumptions and biases and define the criteria of success.
Advance preparation lets risks and unintended consequences be examined without urgency, raising the odds of a quality decision.
quotes: When a high-stakes decision looms large on the horizon, smart leaders talk through the possibilities upstream for several weeks or months before the critical analysis begins.
Without the need to make the decision any time soon, those involved can explore the upside and downside of making the decision in the first place.
Thinking through the premises upon which the eventual decision will be grounded can reveal some valuable insights and biases.
Knowing ahead of time what a decision must accomplish adds a clarity that is hard to achieve later.
If nothing else, the advanced preparation primes the decision-making process for success by getting everyone to think about the decision and giving them the time to let the issues marinate.
As Muhammad Ali used to say, “I run on the road long before I dance under the lights.
